entry: Coming-of-age novel by American author Louisa May Alcott, published in two volumes in 1868 and 1869. It follows the four March sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy, as they pass from childhood to womanhood. Loosely based on the author and her three sisters, it is classified as autobiographical or semi-autobiographical. The book was an immediate commercial and critical success. Alcott wrote two sequels featuring the March sisters, *Little Men* (1871) and *Jo's Boys* (1886), and the two volumes were issued as a single novel in 1880. Scholar Sarah Elbert argues that Alcott combined elements of romantic children's fiction and sentimental novels into a new genre. The novel has been said to address domesticity, work, and true love, and it has been translated into numerous languages and adapted frequently for stage and screen.

Customary public [[Ritual|ritual]] of worship performed by a religious group. Liturgy is a communal response to the sacred, expressing praise, thanksgiving, remembrance, supplication, or repentance, and it forms a basis for establishing a relationship with God or the divine. The word derives from the ancient Greek *leitourgia*, meaning "work or service for the people." In classical Athens, liturgies were costly public duties that wealthy citizens performed to finance festivals and civic amenities. Buddhist liturgy is a formalized service of chanting sutras, mantras, or gathas before objects of veneration, accompanied by offerings of light, incense, water, and food. In [[Christianity]], the term usually refers to a standardized order of events in a sacramental service or service of public prayer. Critics of the distinction between "liturgical" and "non-liturgical" churches argue that even unscripted worship, such as Quaker waiting worship, is liturgical.

Chinese fashion model, described as China's first supermodel. Born in [[Hunan]] Province, she moved to [[Beijing]] at 17 to start her career. In the Fall 2009 season she walked 74 shows, a record for a model of Asian descent in a single season. She was the first Chinese model to walk the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show and the first East Asian spokesmodel for Estée Lauder. In 2017 she became the second Chinese model on the cover of American [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]]. In 2024 she became the first model of Asian descent featured solo on the cover of French Vogue.

Benefit concert held simultaneously in [[London]] and [[Philadelphia]] on July 13, 1985. Organized by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure to raise funds for relief of the 1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia, it grew out of the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" released in December 1984. An estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 nations watched the satellite broadcast, nearly 40 percent of the world population. The BBC World Service program *Assignment* reported in March 2010 that funds had been diverted, but the BBC Editorial Complaints Unit later found "no evidence to support such statements."

Association football club based in [[Liverpool]], England, founded in 1892. It competes in the [[Premier League]]. The club has won a joint-record 20 league titles, eight FA Cups, a record 10 League Cups, and six European Cups. Under Bob Paisley, Joe Fagan, and Kenny Dalglish, it won 11 league titles and four European Cups in the 1970s and 1980s. The 1985 Heysel Stadium disaster in [[Brussels]] killed 39 fans, and English clubs were then banned from European competition for five years. The 1989 Hillsborough disaster killed 97 supporters after grossly negligent policing led to a crowd crush.

Port city and metropolitan borough in Merseyside, England (pop., 2025: 507,915). Established as a borough in Lancashire in 1207, Liverpool became significant in the late 17th century through its heavy involvement in the [[Atlantic slave trade]]. It was a major departure point for emigrants to North America and, at the forefront of the [[Industrial Revolution]], rose to global economic importance. It was granted city status in 1880 and moved to Merseyside in 1974. After decline in the mid-20th century, the [[European Union]] named it European Capital of Culture for 2008, reportedly generating over £800 million for the local economy within a year. The city produced musicians including the [[The Beatles|Beatles]], and it is home to Liverpool Lime Street, the world's oldest still-operating main line railway station. Residents are known as Scousers, and the city has the U.K.'s oldest Black community, Europe's oldest Chinese community, and the first mosque in England.

Non-vascular land plant in the division Marchantiophyta. Liverworts, [[Moss|mosses]], and [[Hornwort|hornworts]] are collectively known as [[Bryophyte|bryophytes]]. Like mosses and hornworts, liverworts have a gametophyte-dominant life cycle in which the [[Sporophyte|sporophyte]] depends on the [[Gametophyte|gametophyte]]. Liverworts are haploid for most of their life cycle, and their sporophytes are short-lived, withering soon after releasing their spores. Some have a flat, branching thallus, while others are leafy. They are distinguished from mosses by single-celled rhizoids, the absence of a midrib in the leaves, and complex oil bodies bounded by membranes. An estimated 9,000 species occur in many terrestrial ecosystems, especially moist tropical regions, though some are adapted to [[Desert|deserts]]. Most liverworts are small, from 2 to 20 millimeters wide.

Domesticated animals raised in an agricultural setting for labor and for products such as meat, eggs, milk, fur, leather, and wool. The term sometimes refers only to animals raised for consumption, or only to farmed ruminants such as cattle, sheep, and goats. The breeding and slaughter of livestock, called [[Animal husbandry|animal husbandry]], has been practiced since humanity's transition to farming. Dogs were domesticated early, appearing in Europe and the Far East about 15,000 years ago, while goats and sheep were domesticated between 11,000 and 5,000 years ago in Southwest Asia. Pigs were domesticated by 8,500 BC in the Near East, and cattle about 10,500 years ago. Modern farming has largely shifted to intensive animal farming, which increases yields but impairs animal welfare, the environment, and public health. Beef, dairy, and sheep are an outsized source of [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] emissions from agriculture.

16th-century conflict over Old Livonia, present-day [[Estonia]] and [[Latvia]]. The war lasted from 1558 to 1583. The [[Tsardom of Russia]] faced a shifting coalition of the Dano-Norwegian Realm, the [[Sweden|Kingdom of Sweden]], and the Union of the [[Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] and the Kingdom of Poland. From 1558 to 1578, Russia dominated the region with early victories at Dorpat (Tartu) and Narva. After Russia dissolved the Livonian Confederation, Poland–Lithuania entered the conflict, and Sweden and Denmark-Norway intervened from 1559 to 1561. In 1576, [[Stephen Báthory]] became king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania and turned the tide, winning the Battle of Wenden in 1578 before campaigning through Russia to the long Siege of Pskov. The 1582 Truce of Jam Zapolski ended the war between Russia and Poland–Lithuania, with Russia losing its Livonian holdings. The following year, the Truce of Plussa gave Sweden most of Ingria and northern Livonia.

Extinct genus of macroraptorial sperm whale from the [[Miocene]] epoch, known mainly from [[Peru]]. Its single species, *Livyatan melvillei*, is named after [[Herman Melville]], author of *Moby-Dick*. The fossils date to about 8.9–9.9 million years ago. The holotype is estimated at 13.5–17.5 meters long, making it one of the largest predators known. Its teeth, up to 36.2 cm long, are the largest biting teeth of any known animal, excluding tusks. It may have competed with the giant shark [[Megalodon|megalodon]] for similar prey. Its extinction was probably caused by a cooling event at the end of the Miocene that reduced food populations.

American actress, singer, and dancer. The daughter of [[Judy Garland]] and director Vincente Minnelli, she is known for her powerful alto voice. She won four Tony Awards, including Best Actress in a Musical for *Flora the Red Menace* (1965) and *The Act* (1978). She received the Academy Award for Best Actress for playing Sally Bowles in the musical film *Cabaret* (1972). Her other honors include a BAFTA Award, an Emmy, and two Golden Globes, and she is one of the few performers to have won an EGOT, completed through an honorary Grammy. Her signature songs include "New York, New York" and "Cabaret."

Informal name for the [[Reptile|reptiles]] known as squamates that are not snakes, encompassing over 7,000 species. Lizards inhabit every continent except [[Antarctica]], as well as most oceanic island chains. They range in size from the 13.5 mm nano-chameleon to the 3-meter-long [[Komodo dragon]]. Most are quadrupedal, and many are territorial, with males signaling in bright colors to attract mates and intimidate rivals. Most are carnivorous ambush predators, although larger [[Monitor lizard|monitor lizards]] can prey on animals as big as water buffalo. Lizards thrive in habitats from [[Wetland|wetlands]] to [[Desert|deserts]] and arctic tundra. Antipredator adaptations include [[Venom|venom]], camouflage, reflex bleeding, and self-amputation of the tail as a decoy. [[Snake|Snakes]] are descended from lizards, so cladistic classifications often treat "lizard" as a paraphyletic group.

American woman acquitted in 1893 of the murders of her father and stepmother in Fall River, Massachusetts. No other individuals were charged. The murders and the 1893 [[Trial|trial]] attracted national publicity and have inspired films, plays, literary works, and [[Rhyme|folk rhymes]]. After the trial, she and her older sister Emma bought a house in the Highlands district of Fall River, where she lived for the rest of her life. Emma moved away after 12 years, to [[New Hampshire]]. Borden died of [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] at age 66.

Capital and largest city of [[Slovenia]], on a trade route between the northern [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]] and the [[Danube]] region. The Roman city of Emona stood on the site, and Ljubljana was first mentioned in the first half of the 12th century. As the historical capital of Carniola, it was under [[Habsburg monarchy|Habsburg]] rule from the Middle Ages until 1918. After [[World War II]] it became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia within Yugoslavia, and it became the capital of independent Slovenia in 1991. Its symbol is the Ljubljana Dragon, shown on the castle tower and on the Dragon Bridge.

Domesticated South American camelid (*Lama glama*), widely used as a meat and pack animal by Andean cultures since the [[Pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian era]]. Llamas are social herd animals whose soft wool contains little lanolin. They learn simple tasks after a few repetitions and can carry about 25 to 30% of their body weight for 8 to 13 km (5–8 miles). DNA analysis indicates that the [[Guanaco]] is the wild ancestor of the llama, while the [[Vicuña]] is the wild ancestor of the alpaca. The ancestors of llamas originated on the [[Great Plains]] of North America about 40 million years ago and migrated to [[South America]] about three million years ago. As of 2007, there were over seven million llamas and alpacas in South America. In Aymara mythology, the Heavenly Llama is said to drink water from the ocean and urinate as rain.

Soil composed mostly of [[Sand|sand]], silt, and a smaller amount of [[Clay|clay]], roughly 40–40–20% by weight. In the U.S. Department of Agriculture's textural classification, loam is the only class that is not predominantly sand, silt, or clay. Loam holds more nutrients, moisture, and humus than sandy soils, drains better than silt- or clay-rich soils, and is easier to till than clay. It is considered ideal for gardening and farming, though compaction or loss of organic matter can degrade it. Loam has been used in construction since ancient times, in traditional loam post-and-beam houses, rammed earth, and adobe bricks.

Transfer of money or other assets from a lender to a borrower under an agreement to repay, usually with [[Interest (economics)|interest]]. The borrower incurs a debt, and interest gives the lender an incentive to lend. The promissory note evidencing the debt usually specifies the principal, the interest rate, and the repayment date, and the terms are enforced by [[Contract|contract]], which may also impose loan covenants. Lending is a main activity of [[Bank|banks]] and [[Credit card|credit card]] companies, while other institutions often raise funds by issuing [[Bond (finance)|bonds]]. A secured loan is backed by collateral: in a [[Mortgage|mortgage]], the lender holds a lien on the property until it is paid off and may repossess and sell it after a default. Interest rates on unsecured loans, such as personal loans, credit cards, and overdrafts, are nearly always higher, because the lender's recourse is limited to suing the borrower and enforcing a judgment against unencumbered assets.

Discredited neurosurgical procedure, also called leucotomy, that severs nerve connections in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. Used from the 1930s until the 1970s to treat [[Mental disorder|psychiatric disorders]] in some countries, it was pioneered by Portuguese neurologist António Egas Moniz, who shared the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Walter Freeman popularized it in the United States, where almost 20,000 lobotomies had been performed by 1951. The procedure reduced symptoms at the expense of personality and intellect. It was abandoned from the 1950s onward, first in the [[Soviet Union]], where it was banned in December 1950, and then in Europe.

Marine [[Decapod|decapod]] [[Crustacean|crustacean]] of the family Nephropidae, with a long body, a muscular tail, and large claws. Lobsters live in crevices or burrows on the sea floor. Three of their five pairs of legs bear claws, and the first pair is usually much larger than the others. Highly prized as [[Seafood|seafood]], lobsters are among the most profitable commodities in the coastal areas they populate. Like other [[Arthropod|arthropods]], they must shed their hard exoskeletons to grow, and several species change color during molting. Their blue blood comes from [[Copper|copper]]-containing hemocyanin rather than the iron-rich [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]] of vertebrates. The unqualified term refers to clawed lobsters; spiny lobsters and squat lobsters are not closely related to them.

Galaxy group containing the [[Milky Way]], where [[Earth]] is located. Its two main collections of galaxies form a "dumbbell" shape: the Milky Way and its satellites form one lobe, and the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] and its satellites form the other. The lobes are about 800 kiloparsecs apart and are moving toward one another at 123 km/s. The two largest members, both spiral galaxies, each have masses of about 10¹² solar masses. The [[Triangulum Galaxy]] (M33) is the third-largest member. Most of the 134 known members are dwarf galaxies, and the exact number is unknown because the Milky Way obscures some. The group is part of the Local Volume and the larger [[Virgo Supercluster]], which is part of the [[Laniakea Supercluster]].

Large freshwater loch in the [[Scottish Highlands]]. It lies along the Great Glen Fault and forms part of the Caledonian Canal, which links the east and west coasts of Scotland. Stretching about 37 km (23 miles), it is the second-largest Scottish loch by surface area after Loch Lomond, but the largest by volume in the British Isles, with more water than all the lakes in England and Wales combined. Its deepest point is 754 feet (229.8 meters). Peat in the surrounding soil makes its water exceptionally murky. The loch is best known for claimed sightings of the [[Loch Ness Monster]].

Mythical creature in Scottish folklore, said to inhabit a [[Loch Ness|loch]] in the [[Scottish Highlands]]. Known affectionately as "Nessie," it is described as large and long-necked, with one or more humps above the water. It was brought to worldwide attention in 1933. The earliest account, in *Life of St. Columba* by Adomnán, written in the 7th century, describes a water beast attacking a man in the River Ness rather than the loch itself. Evidence is anecdotal, including disputed photographs and sonar readings, and scientists attribute the sightings to hoaxes, misidentified animals, and other natural phenomena.

Fastening device released by a physical key, keycard, or [[Fingerprint|fingerprint]], or by secret information such as a [[Password|password]], and the key that operates it. A typical key is a small piece of metal with a bit that slides into the keyway and a bow that allows torque to be applied. Common metals include [[Brass|brass]], nickel silver, and [[Steel|steel]]. Locks have been in use for over 6,000 years, and an early example was found in the ruins of [[Nineveh]], the capital of ancient [[Assyria]]. The Egyptian wooden pin lock lifted pins out of drilled holes to release the bolt when a key was inserted. The Romans invented metal locks and keys. In 1778 Robert Barron invented the lever tumbler lock, which Jeremiah Chubb greatly improved in 1818. Opening a lock without a key is called lock picking.

Chamber for raising and lowering boats between stretches of water at different levels on rivers and [[Canal|canals]]. Locks make a river more navigable or allow a canal to cross uneven land. The most common type is the pound lock, with a watertight chamber, a gate at each end, and gear to fill and empty the chamber. Pound locks first appeared in medieval China during the [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279). In 984, the tax administrator Qiao Weiyue installed a pair of sluice gates 250 feet apart, effectively creating a pound lock. The first true European pound lock was built in 1396 at Damme near [[Bruges]], Belgium. Passing through a lock usually takes 10 to 20 minutes, depending on the size of the lock and the water level on arrival.

American four-engined turboprop military transport aircraft. Capable of using unprepared runways, it was designed as a troop, medical evacuation, and cargo aircraft. Variants serve as gunships (AC-130) and for [[Aerial refueling|aerial refueling]], search and rescue, weather reconnaissance, and aerial firefighting. Designed by Lockheed (now [[Lockheed Martin]]), it entered U.S. Air Force service in 1956 and was followed by [[Australia]] and many other nations. More than 40 variants operate in more than 60 nations. It is the longest continuously produced military aircraft, with 70 years of production as of 2024.
